headline: SKI enables voice coding for AI agents, speeding up developer workflow.
summary: SKI is a free tool that lets developers interact with AI coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor using voice, eliminating the need for constant typing and checking. It offers a faster, more natural way to code.
details: SKI is a new free tool that lets developers use voice to interact with AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor. It aims to replace the traditional type-wait-check loop with a more fluid conversational approach.

With SKI, users speak their commands, and the AI agent responds audibly, mimicking natural conversation. This direct voice input and output streamline the coding process, making it feel more intuitive.

Setting up SKI involves downloading the tool for Mac (Apple Silicon, macOS 14.4+) or Windows (x64) and installing its "skill" into your preferred coding agent with a single click. No Linux build is available yet.

The tool transcribes voice locally and passes it to the agent as if typed, ensuring privacy as no voice or code is uploaded. The agent can then speak up for decisions or when tasks are complete, allowing for continuous voice interaction.
SKI is built specifically for the agent loop, supporting a wide range of coding agents. It currently operates in English only and requires Apple Silicon on Mac.

The core voice loop functionality is free for life, with no caps or credit card required. An optional paid add-on, AgentCall, allows agents to join live Zoom/Meet/Teams calls, though local meeting recording and transcription are free.
caption:

headline_marked: [[Lint your AI prompts first]] to stop wasting free model calls
headline: Lint your AI prompts first to stop wasting free model calls
summary: Free model access can hide significant waste from repeated bad prompts. Implementing a static contract check for prompts before model calls can prevent this inefficiency.
details: Repeated calls to free AI models can quickly deplete your token budget if prompts are ambiguous. One developer found their pipeline calling a free model three times on the same commit due to unclear instructions, wasting resources.
The core issue isn't the model, but the prompt itself. A prompt acts as a contract between the developer and the model; a vague contract leads to vague or incorrect output.
The proposed solution is a 'static contract check' or linter for prompts. This gate runs before the model is called, quickly verifying the prompt's structure, not its correctness.
This linter prevents unnecessary model calls by stopping the pipeline if the prompt file changes and fails the check. It's designed to catch 'cheap mistakes' without consuming model tokens.
The linter can be used locally for small projects or deployed as a tiny HTTP endpoint for CI/CD pipelines, keeping runner images clean and checks stable across multiple projects.

While not making the model smarter, this approach effectively prevents the model from being asked bad questions repeatedly. It's most useful when prompts are stored in the repository and not generated at runtime.
